title: Rate rise still in play despite jobless spike
full_text:
A rise in the unemployment rate to its equal-highest level in almost five years last month suggests the economy is softening at a faster clip than economists expected - but not enough to rule out the chance of another interest rate rise this year.
The unemployment rate rose 0.1 percentage points to 4.5 per cent in July - the equal-highest level since November 2021 - as 15,800 people lost work.
The figures came in weaker than expected on the back of the Reserve Bank of Australia's three interest rate rises this year.
Before the release on Thursday, consensus forecasts had expected the jobless rate to hold steady at 4.4 per cent, with 12,000 more people finding employment.
The labour market softening was broad-based, with the underemployment rate - the share of people with jobs who would like to work more hours - ticking up to a two-year high of 6.4 per cent, while the number of hours worked in all jobs for the month fell by 1 million.
"This is a pretty clear indication that there is increasing slack in the labour market, and this should support disinflation," said Nick Stenner, Bank of America's head of Australia and New Zealand economics, about the rise in underemployment.
The participation rate and the employment-to-population ratio both fell by 0.2 per cent in July to 66.9 per cent and 63.9 per cent, respectively.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers downplayed the rise in unemployment on Thursday. "It's unsurprising to see unemployment tick up a bit given the challenges coming at us from around the world," said Chalmers.
Thursday's data was not the first indication that the labour market could be cooling faster than expected.
As Stenner noted, the uptick in the unemployment rate was consistent with the wage growth data released on Wednesday by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, which showed private-sector wages grew 3.1 per cent for the year to June, their slowest annual pace since 2022.
"The weakness in private-sector wages is actually consistent with an unemployment rate in the low-to-mid 5 per cent range," said Stenner.
The Reserve Bank of Australia also increased its longer-dated unemployment forecasts in August on the back of a higher starting rate than its economists previously expected.
The central bank now expects the unemployment rate to rise to 4.8 per cent by June 2028, and to remain there through the second half of that year. That is significantly higher than the government's forecasts, handed down with the federal budget in May, for unemployment to hit 4.5 per cent in 2028.
PwC Australia chief economist Amy Lomas said the Reserve Bank's monetary policy board was likely to be pleasantly surprised by Thursday's numbers, given the data shows the cooling in the labour market is broad-based enough to help drive down inflation, yet gradual enough not to stoke public concern.
"It's heading in the right direction at a nice rate, which is acceptable to the community and acceptable to the Reserve Bank," said Lomas.
She said the marginal fall in the participation rate left it as the one measure that still seemed "pretty strong".
The Victorian unemployment rate steadied at 5.1 per cent, its highest level since the COVID-19 pandemic, while NSW's rate was almost a percentage point lower at 4.2 per cent, despite a 0.3 percentage point increase.
On Wednesday, RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser echoed governor Michele Bullock's warning that the monetary policy board would have little choice but to raise interest rates if consumption and employment growth did not slow.
"We've seen a little bit of that [slowdown] so far," said Hauser. "We're going to need to see more to get inflation back."
The 80,200-strong jump in employment last month smashed market expectations and bolstered fears of another interest rate rise. However, economists scaled back those calls following a muted inflation report the following week.
The soft employment report pushed traders to modestly reduce their bets on a fourth interest rate rise this year, cognisant that the RBA will need more evidence of an economic slowdown - including in next week's inflation report - to keep the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent.
After the numbers were released, bond markets were pricing in a 16 per cent chance of a borrowing cost increase at the monetary policy board's September meeting, rising to a 53 per cent chance by December.
That is down from 20 per cent and 62 per cent respectively before the data was released on Thursday.
